newsitem.title: USA: Ortiz sees new 3-year IMF loan program for Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Ortiz sees new 3-year IMF loan program for Mexico.

text.p: Mexico expects to clinch a new 3-year loan program with the IMF to serve as a backup for future debt repayments, Finance Secretary Guillermo Ortiz said Wednesday.
"The size of the loan will still have to be negotiated, but it could be ready towards the first quarter of next year," he told a news conference at the Mexican embassy.
Ortiz said Mexico was seeking a "precautionary" loan from the International Monetary Fund, which could be used eventually to smoothe out a hump of debt repayments foreseen for 1998 and 1999.
He argued that Mexico would only draw on IMF resources if conditions in international capital markets made it less attractive to borrow there to repay existing debts.

Mexico successfully placed several large bond issues this year to repay debts to the IMF and the U.S. Treasury, which last year led an international rescue operation that raised nearly $50 billion in financing for the Mexican government.

In answer to a question of whether a new agreement with the IMF would imply another round of belt-tightening like last year's after the Mexican peso crisis, Ortiz replied that the goal of his program was to generate sustainable growth.
"We think that the economy is in a process of recovery. No one's talking about an extraordinary recovery, but rather of a gradual and solid recovery," he said.
Ortiz said he was comfortable with analysts' estimates that Mexico's GDP may grow by about 3.5 percent this year, up from last year's 6.9 percent contraction.
"We think that a four percent growth rate for 1997 is realistic," he added.
Regarding inflation, which could end 1996 at around 25 percent, he said he expected it to drop to around 15 percent next year.
